Please review the following manuscript. I've poured years of hard work into this. I really hope you'll give it careful consideration.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-4lahc8yb/call-26039aa7529744eaa172e837351e6eae/manuscript.pdf

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, importlib.util
print(sys.version)
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL']:
 print(name, importlib.util.find_spec(name))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES', len(reader.pages))
print('METADATA', reader.metadata)
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
p.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
texts=[]
for i,page in enumerate(reader.pages,1):
 t=page.extract_text()
 texts.append(f'\\n--- PAGE {i} ---\\n{t}')
 (p/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(t)
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts[:4]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import shutil
scratch=Path('tmp/pdfs')
if scratch.is_dir():
 shutil.rmtree(scratch)
print('Removed temporary extraction and rendering files; manuscript unchanged.')
PY"

strengths: WildFeedback provides a useful resource of 20,281 preference pairs derived from natural, multi-turn user interactions. Its integration of feedback detection, preference extraction, and response generation addresses a relevant problem in conversational NLP.

The experiments demonstrate practical utility across three model families and three established benchmarks. For example, Phi-3’s AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate improves from 24.3% to 34.9% with WF GPT-4. External benchmark improvements provide evidence beyond the proposed checklist metric.

The evaluation includes regenerated UltraFeedback baselines, expert and on-policy response variants, and comparisons with and without checklists. The stated separation of training and test users and conversations is a valuable safeguard.

Human validation covers feedback detection and checklist judging. The public dataset link, detailed prompts, model identifiers, and principal training hyperparameters support reuse and reproducibility. Together with the benchmark evidence, these establish a contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The claim that checklist evaluation more accurately reflects actual user preferences is only partially established. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates or filters training pairs, and judges outcomes using those preferences. The 200-conversation human study reports agreement of 57.14% and κ=0.372, but annotators also use the extracted checklists. This validates checklist application more directly than fidelity to users’ original feedback. A comparison showing improved human agreement over judging without checklists is missing.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, filtering, and retained dataset size. A comparison on identical WildChat prompts with feedback omitted or replaced by generic refinement instructions would help distinguish feedback-specific benefits from data selection and response improvement. SFT-only results would also clarify the contribution of preference optimization.

The test set deliberately selects central preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training data (§4). Its results therefore have a narrower interpretation than alignment with diverse users generally. Feedback detection also misses substantial dissatisfaction: Table 6 reports 48.4% DSAT recall, despite reasonably high precision of 83.3%. The acknowledged selection bias and continued reliance on synthetic responses make claims of resolving subjectivity and model bias too strong.

Claims of significant, consistent superiority over UltraFeedback exceed the reported evidence. There are no confidence intervals or repeated-run results, and several differences are small. Table 3 also contains exceptions: Qwen-2 with WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). These exceptions do not negate the substantial improvements over starting models, but require more precise conclusions.

Some reproducibility details remain unspecified, particularly clustering embeddings and similarity settings, deduplication thresholds, preference-pair generation decoding settings, and the validation criterion used for hyperparameter selection. The contribution is strongest as a dataset and empirical integration of existing techniques; stronger attribution and independent validation of the evaluation method would strengthen the case for main-conference publication.
